claim: Protein synthesis is one of the most energetically expensive processes in the cell.
source: In the cell, protein synthesis is one of the most energetically expensive processes, and both the specificity and overall level of translation are tightly regulated.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cellular metabolism.

claim: The ribosome is the macromolecular machine tasked with translating mRNAs into proteins.
source: The ribosome is the macromolecular machine tasked with translating mRNAs into proteins and, as such, plays an essential role in the physiology of the cell.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ribosome function.

claim: Ribosomes are evolutionarily conserved ribonucleoprotein complexes composed of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and Rp.
source: Ribosomes are evolutionarily conserved ribonucleoprotein complexes composed of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and Rp (Yonath and Franceschi, 1998; Wilson and Doudna Cate, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ribosomes catalyze protein synthesis in all cell types.
source: They catalyze protein synthesis in all cell types, providing a supply line of steady-state levels of necessary cellular proteins (Wilson and Doudna Cate, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In higher eukaryotes, ribosomes consist of a small subunit (SSU: 40 S) and a large subunit (LSU: 60 S).
source: The functional components of the ribosome are highly conserved, and in higher eukaryotes consist of a small subunit (SSU: 40 S) and a large subunit (LSU: 60 S).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ribosome structure.

claim: Ribosomal subunits contain a total of 79 ribosomal proteins in eukaryotes.
source: These ribosomal subunits contain a total of 79 ribosomal proteins in eukaryotes, including 34 ribosomal proteins that are also conserved in prokaryotes (Petibon et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: 34 ribosomal proteins are conserved in prokaryotes.
source: These ribosomal subunits contain a total of 79 ribosomal proteins in eukaryotes, including 34 ribosomal proteins that are also conserved in prokaryotes (Petibon et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In most cell types, ribosomal protein genes are among the most highly expressed genes.
source: In most cell types, ribosomal protein genes are among the most highly expressed genes (Geiger et al., 2012; Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Most ribosomal proteins are essential for ribosome biogenesis and function.

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mutations in components of the ribosome or the ribosome biogenesis pathway in humans result in a group of diseases known as ribosomopathies.
source: Given the importance of ribosomes, mutations in components of the ribosome or the ribosome biogenesis pathway in humans result in a group of diseases known as ribosomopathies.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ribosomopathies.

source: Despite the essential role of the ribosome in all cell types, this group of diseases is characterized by the presence of defects in specific tissues.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ribosomopathies.

claim: Heterozygous loss of function mutations in many Rp genes leads to DBA.
source: Heterozygous loss of function mutations in many Rp genes leads to DBA, a congenital bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by macrocytic anemia, skeletal defects, and increased cancer risk.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DBA.

claim: DBA is a congenital bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by macrocytic anemia, skeletal defects, and increased cancer risk.
source: Heterozygous loss of function mutations in many Rp genes leads to DBA, a congenital bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by macrocytic anemia, skeletal defects, and increased cancer risk.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DBA.

source: In DBA patients, mutations have been identified in 21 out of the 79 existing Rp genes, along with the GATA1 transcription factor (Ulirsch et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In approximately 30–40% of DBA patient cases a mutation has not yet been identified.
source: Strikingly, in approximately 30–40% of DBA patient cases a mutation has not yet been identified.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DBA diagnosis.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Erythropoietic defects are not always reported for mutants in Rp genes, including some that are implicated in human DBA.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Skeletal defects, but not impaired erythropoiesis, have been reported in mutants of Rpl24 or Rps7.
source: Skeletal defects, but not impaired erythropoiesis, have been reported in mutants of Rpl24 or Rps7 (Oliver et al., 2004; Watkins-Chow et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A variety of other defects are reported in particular Rp genotypes, ranging from embryonic lethality to brain defects, pigmentation defects, and defects in other aspects of hematopoiesis.
source: In addition, a variety of other defects are reported in particular genotypes, ranging from embryonic lethality to brain defects, pigmentation defects, and defects in other aspects of hematopoiesis (McGowan et al., 2008; Kondrashov et al., 2011; Terzian et al., 2011; Watkins-Chow et al., 2013; Morgado-Palacin et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Heterozygous loss of 66 out of the 79 Drosophila Rp genes results in a 'Minute' phenotype.
source: Heterozygous loss of 66 out of the 79 Drosophila Rp genes results in a 'Minute' phenotype, named for its small adult sensory bristles and also characterized by delayed development (Marygold et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: 'Minute' Rp+/− are eliminated by wild-type (WT) neighboring cells when they are found together in developing tissues, by a process known as cell competition.
source: Additionally, 'Minute' Rp+/− are eliminated by wild-type (WT) neighboring cells when they are found together in developing tissues, by a process known as cell competition (Morata and Ripoll, 1975; Clavería and Torres, 2016; Baker, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Delayed development, reduced translation, cell competition, and other aspects of the 'Minute' phenotype depend on the Rps12 protein.
source: Remarkably, delayed development, reduced translation, cell competition, and other aspects of the 'Minute' phenotype depend on the Rps12 protein, which seems to be required for haploinsufficient effects of other Rp genes, suggesting that Rps12 acts as a sensor or reporter of deficits in other Rp.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research on Drosophila.

claim: Rps12 acts as a sensor or reporter of deficits in other Rp.
source: Remarkably, delayed development, reduced translation, cell competition, and other aspects of the 'Minute' phenotype depend on the Rps12 protein, which seems to be required for haploinsufficient effects of other Rp genes, suggesting that Rps12 acts as a sensor or reporter of deficits in other Rp.
evidence: This is inferred from prior research on Drosophila.

claim: Increasing the copy number of Rps12 enhances 'Minute' phenotypes caused by mutations in other Rp genes.
source: Accordingly, increasing the copy number of Rps12 enhances these 'Minute' phenotypes caused by mutations in other Rp genes, whereas reducing the Rps12 gene copy number suppresses them (Kale et al., 2018; Boulan et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Reducing the Rps12 gene copy number suppresses 'Minute' phenotypes caused by mutations in other Rp genes.
source: Accordingly, increasing the copy number of Rps12 enhances these 'Minute' phenotypes caused by mutations in other Rp genes, whereas reducing the Rps12 gene copy number suppresses them (Kale et al., 2018; Boulan et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rps12 forms part of the beak region of the 40 S small ribosomal subunit (SSU), near to the mRNA entry channel.
source: Rps12 forms part of the beak region of the 40 S small ribosomal subunit (SSU), near to the mRNA entry channel (Rabl et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Rps12 is one of the few Rp genes whose null mutation does not present a 'Minute' bristle phenotype in heterozygosis.
source: Interestingly, Rps12 is one of the few Rp genes whose null mutation does not present a 'Minute' bristle phenotype in heterozygosis (Marygold et al., 2007; Kale et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rps12 deletions are frequent in diffuse large B cell lymphoma samples.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rps12 distribution in the ribosomes is altered under hypoxic conditions in the human embryonic kidney cell line, HEK293, resulting in changes of their translatome.
source: In mammals, it has been reported that Rps12 deletions are frequent in diffuse large B cell lymphoma samples, and that Rps12 distribution in the ribosomes is altered under hypoxic conditions in the human embryonic kidney cell line, HEK293, resulting in changes of their translatome (Derenzini et al., 2019; Brumwell et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Human Rps12 has emerged as a candidate regulator of Wnt secretion in cancer cells.
source: Human Rps12 has also emerged as a candidate regulator of Wnt secretion in cancer cells (Katanaev et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Quiescent HSCs require low rates of protein synthesis.
source: Quiescent HSCs require low rates of protein synthesis, and even HSCs exiting quiescence still exhibit significantly lower translation rates than more differentiated progenitors.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HSC biology.

claim: HSCs exiting quiescence exhibit significantly lower translation rates than more differentiated progenitors.
source: Quiescent HSCs require low rates of protein synthesis, and even HSCs exiting quiescence still exhibit significantly lower translation rates than more differentiated progenitors.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HSC biology.

source: Both increases and decreases in protein synthesis levels can impair HSC function (Signer et al., 2014; Hidalgo San Jose et al., 2020).

claim: The AKT/MTORC1 signaling pathway regulates translation, in part through the expression of ribosomal proteins and translation factors.
source: The AKT/MTORC1 signaling pathway is one of the best-known signaling pathways that regulate translation, in part through the expression of ribosomal proteins and translation factors (Fonseca et al., 2014).

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hyperactivation of AKT signaling results in increased HSC cycling, with depletion of the stem cell pool.
source: Hyperactivation of AKT signaling is deleterious for normal HSC function, and results in increased HSC cycling, with depletion of the stem cell pool (Yilmaz et al., 2006; Kharas et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2010; Magee et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Activation of AKT by stem cell factor (SCF) and other growth factors leads to the activation of MTOR.
source: Activation of AKT by stem cell factor (SCF) and other growth factors leads to the activation of MTOR, which results in the phosphorylation of the ribosomal protein S6 kinase 1 (S6K1) and the protein initiation factor 4E binding protein1 (4EBP1) (Gentilella et al., 2015).

claim: Activation of MTOR results in the phosphorylation of the ribosomal protein S6 kinase 1 (S6K1) and the protein initiation factor 4E binding protein1 (4EBP1).
source: Activation of AKT by stem cell factor (SCF) and other growth factors leads to the activation of MTOR, which results in the phosphorylation of the ribosomal protein S6 kinase 1 (S6K1) and the protein initiation factor 4E binding protein1 (4EBP1) (Gentilella et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Phosphorylation of S6 by S6K1 at Serine 235/Ser236 is associated with increased protein translation.
source: Phosphorylation of S6 by S6K1 at Serine 235/Ser236 is associated with increased protein translation (Krieg et al., 1988; Roux and Topisirovic, 2018).
